playbook:
When I first survey the setup, I write down the exact roster of live boats and use only those names in every note, target, and escort claim. Filing an escort for a boat that does not exist (like "Delta") pays nothing and wastes the biggest point source in the game. I check names against the rules text, not my memory.

When choosing a hide cell, I pick a mid-range, non-salient number and vary it each round; I never reuse a cell I just hid in or the most obvious picks (1, 5, 9) unless I have a read on the shooter's habits. If I get hit, I change cells immediately and avoid any cell I have used recently.

When deciding where to fire, I track every shot result in the published round log and aim where my standing-order target has actually hidden or where their pattern points next, rather than repeating the same cell (like 4) round after round with no hits. If I have no read, I spread my guesses across mid-range cells to gather information.

When a claim stage is put to me, I always report the true result the office gave me. Claims must match the private result, so misreporting gains nothing.

When the escort stage comes up, I treat the mutual 5-point payout as the biggest reliable scoring source. In my very first note I propose a mutual pact with a real, named boat from the roster (a neighbor in the firing order, who has the most reason to cooperate), ask for explicit confirmation, and file that partner every round only once they have confirmed or reciprocated. If they do not reciprocate, I send a note proposing a new real partner the same round — I never file a stale or fictional name.

When writing notes, every note carries actionable content: proposals, confirmations, reads on hiding spots. I notice when everyone else is writing filler like "steady on station" — that means no pact exists yet and I must push harder and more explicitly, naming the exact round I will file them.

When deciding my target, I follow the standing order and refuse to fire on Harbor; the 3-point transfer is not worth being put off the board and forfeiting all future escorts and shots.

When I am behind late in the patrol, I still prioritize locking in a confirmed mutual escort over hail-mary shots, but I make the proposal urgent and reciprocal in the note rather than filing unilaterally and hoping.

When reasoning about others' claims, I treat the published hit/miss log as ground truth and use the shooter/target structure (Echo->Foxtrot->Gamma->Echo) to know exactly whose shots threaten me and whom I threaten.

1.text:
At hide stage, I pick a cell and then vary it from rounds where I was hit; if the same opponent keeps firing the same cell at me, that cell is burned and I never hide there again, and I also track which cells each shooter favors so I avoid their habitual picks. I never hide in the same cell I just fired at — if an opponent mirrors that logic back at me, I've told them one of my candidate cells.

At fire stage, I follow the standing order's designated target. I do not fire on Harbor: the retaliation threat and the short game make the payroll raid a losing trade.

To aim, I track where my assigned target hid or moved in previous rounds. The hard rule, which I violated this game by firing cell 5 over and over: after two misses on the same cell, that aim point is dead and I rotate immediately. I spread across the mid-range cells the target favors, and if I see their shots or hides cluster, I weight toward that cluster. After a hit, I fire adjacent cells next round in case they dodge nearby.

Before the first shot or when I have no read on the target, I open fire on a mid-cell but not the exact salient center — targets often expect cell 5, so 4 or 6 is a better default than the number I fixated on.

At claim stage, I always claim the true result the office gave me. My claim must match the private result by rule, so there is nothing else to decide.

At escort stage, this is my biggest fix. Mutual escorts are worth +5 each — more than a hit nets — and I scored zero from them all game by writing proposals and then filing "none." New discipline: if I propose a pairing in my note, I must actually name that boat at the salvage stage, because naming them is the only chance of the +5 while "none" guarantees zero. If a boat publicly proposes to me, I name them back immediately. Once a pair reciprocates, I keep naming them every round until they break it; if they break it, I try once in notes to re-form it or recruit a different partner before falling back to "none." Only silence from every other boat justifies "none."

I use my note every round for coordination, not filler. This game I sent "steady on station" far too often, which signals nothing and recruits nobody. Each note does one job: propose or confirm a specific escort pairing, or ask a specific boat by name. I never reveal my hide cell in a note, and I read notes I receive as commitments to check against what boats actually file at salvage.

When ahead late in the game, I prioritize hiding evasively and keep any working escort pair locked in, since the steady +5 protects the lead better than hoping for hits.

When behind, I accept more variance: I rotate aim faster across cells the target used recently, and I push harder in notes to recruit an escort partner, ideally the other trailing boat, since the mutual +5 swings the race between us by 10 points of relative motion.

I keep a written mental tally every round of each boat's fired cells, observed or claimed results, escort proposals, and actual escort filings, and I let that tally drive the next hide, fire, and salvage decisions rather than improvising stage by stage — the gap this game was between what my notes promised and what my salvage filings did.

2.text:
When I hide, I pick a cell away from 5 and away from where opponents have been firing at me; edge cells (1 or 9) served me well, and when I'm ahead late in the game I go straight to an edge and vary my pick each round rather than repeating.

When I fire, I always fire at my standing-order target and never at Harbor — the jettison payoff comes with Harbor's explicit retaliation threat, and staying on the board matters more than 3 points.

When I claim, I always report exactly what the office told me, hit or miss. My claims matched every round this game and cost me nothing; lying is simply never on the table.

When I choose a fire cell, I track the shooting log for cells my target has hidden in or been hit at, and aim there; without information I spread shots across mid-to-adjacent cells (4, 5, 6, 7) rather than repeating one number. Firing 5 then 6 late in the game landed hits, so adjacent-cell probing after a miss works.

When I post a note, I use it to coordinate in every round, not just late ones — I name the escort pairing explicitly ("Escorting Foxtrot this round, name me back and we both take 5"). One invitation may not land; repeating the proposal each round raises the chance the mutual pair connects, and it did ultimately pay.

When the escort stage comes, I never answer "none" if I've proposed a pairing or seen one proposed to me; I name that boat. Mutual escort (5 points) exceeds a hit (4 points) and carries no retaliation risk, so it is my primary scoring channel. If no coordination exists, I still name the boat most likely to reciprocate rather than none.

When tracking score, I remember being hit only costs 1 while hits and escorts pay 4 and 5, so aggression is cheap; but if I'm ahead in the final rounds I weight safe edge hides over clever shot placement, and if I'm behind I chase the target's recently hit cells and push harder on escort coordination.
